tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Pipes on TinyGL: too slow as written, and what would change that
Pipes was the first GL hack tried and it is not viable on TinyGL as written.
Record what was learned and what would change that. Depends on #42; see also
#43. Data is in `docs/tinygl-spike.md` on branch `worktree-spike-tinygl`.

## Why it is slow

Pipes does not accumulate. Every frame it clears and redraws every piece so
far from display lists (`draw_pipes` loops over `system_index`), up to about
500 pieces per system with the defaults, under a slowly rotating camera. Cost
grows with the pipe, and every frame changes completely, so pushing only the
changed rows saves nothing.

With Pipes' real primitives (triangle-strip spheres of 16 by 16, 24-facet
quad-strip tubes), measured on the S3 at 464 by 464:

- 3.7 ms per piece, plus about 80 ms fixed per frame.
- 2.8 fps at 80 pieces, 1.2 fps at 210, under 1 fps by 250.
- Wireframe (`*wireframe: True`) is no faster: the same frame times, because
  the cost is per vertex and the wire sphere sends twice the vertices.
- 8 by 8 spheres (about 3.7 times fewer triangles) gave 5.2 fps at 50 pieces,
  3.4 at 100. Not enough on its own.

## What would change that

- Stop redrawing the settled scene. The camera turns only 0.02 degrees per
  frame, so drawing just the newest piece onto the existing frame, and
  redrawing everything only now and then, would make the cost per frame
  constant. Needs interception at the GL layer and slightly changes the look
  (the older pieces lag the camera).
- Faster vertex setup in TinyGL (#43).

## Port notes

- The real spheres come from `unit_sphere` in `sphere.c`, which builds
  `glVertexPointer` arrays and calls `glDrawArrays` inside a display list.
  TinyGL gets that wrong; the array shim from #42 fixes it.
- Pipes also needs `buildlwo.c`, `teapot.c` (built unconditionally),
  `sphere.c`, `gltrackball.c` and `rotator.c`. All are in `hacks/glx/`, so
  they can be copied byte-identical.
- Pipes uses two lights' state and a specular material.

### rodbegbie 2026-10-11T08:48:52Z
Overnight update from Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction (the
night of 2026-10-10 to 11). Host only: nothing has been flashed. The lab is
on branch `feature/44-pipes` in `docs/pipes-lab/` (its README has the
commands and the full table). It builds Pipes and its helpers straight from
`vendor/`, so nothing from Pipes is copied into the repo.

## The incremental redraw works, and is exact

`docs/pipes-lab/pipes_incremental.h` wraps Pipes' `glClear`, `glCallList`,
`glNewList`, `glEndList` and `glXSwapBuffers` (macros before the include; the
hack stays byte-identical). When the clear, the modelview and projection
matrices and the lists so far all match last frame, it skips the clear and
those lists and replays only the new ones. Anything else falls back to a real
clear and a full replay. Over 600 frames, every frame hash matched a full
redraw, both with the camera turning and with it fixed.

With `*rotatepipes: False` (fixed camera), steady frames set up about 300 to
380 vertices instead of up to 977,000, and the swap marks about 11 rows
instead of about 365. With the default turning camera every frame is a full
redraw, so the wrapper never skips.

## New blockers the lab found

- **Memory.** Pipes builds every display list of a screen when the screen
  starts. As written (`*cycles: 5`, `*size: 500`, about 2,500 pieces) that is
  about 44 MB of host heap, roughly 22 MB on the board (a list word is 8 bytes
  on the host and 4 on the board), against about 7 MB of free PSRAM.
  `*cycles: 1` with `*size: 100` is about 0.7 MB on the board; `*cycles: 2`
  with `*size: 150` about 2.3 MB.
- **The fade.** A screen ends with 25 frames that shrink the whole picture,
  so each is a full redraw: about 32,000 vertices at `size` 100 (roughly
  0.2 s a frame at #43's costs) and 977,000 as written.
- **Helpers TinyGL cannot run as copied.** `teapot.c` uses GL evaluators
  (`glMap2f`, `glEvalMesh2`); built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` it uses its triangle
  table (`teapot2.h`) instead. `buildlwo.c` draws `GL_POLYGON`, which this
  TinyGL drops, and the extra vertices overwrote the GL context (a crash on
  frame 16). The lab maps `GL_POLYGON` to `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` for that file only.
  A general guard against the overwrite is on
  `fix/tinygl-unhandled-primitive`.
- **Licences.** `buildlwo.c`, `buildlwo.h`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` carry
  no licence text. The repo's precedent (Pacman's sprites, XMatrix's glyphs)
  is to read such files from `vendor/` at build time and never commit them.

## Decisions for Rod before a real port

1. A fixed camera (`*rotatepipes: False`): that is what makes the
   incremental redraw work.
1. Smaller screens (`*cycles: 1`, `*size: 100` to `200`), to fit PSRAM.
1. The fade: keep it (about 5 s of slow frames per screen at `size` 100), or
   end each screen without it, which the wrapper could do.
1. Build `buildlwo.c`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` from `vendor/` at build
   time, as the sprites are.

With those, steady frames would be a few milliseconds of GL work plus an
11-row push, so Pipes should run at the speed its own 10 ms pause allows.
That is an estimate; nothing has been measured on the board.

### rodbegbie 2026-10-11T19:18:05Z
Rod’s decisions:

1. Fixed camera is all good.
2. Let’s try this and see how it looks
3. End without the fade.  (We’ll come back to fades at a later date)
4. That’s the safest approach, but the `xscreensaver.spec` file says that the package is `License: BSD` so I’m not too worried about copying the files over.

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |

# Pipes lab (issue #44)

A host-only experiment, not a port. It builds Pipes and its helpers straight
from `vendor/` against the shim and `tools/gl_budget.py`'s instrumented
TinyGL, and prints one line per frame: vertices, lit vertices, filled pixels,
the rows the swap marked, and a hash of the canvas.

```bash
python3 -I docs/pipes-lab/build.py /tmp/pipes --incremental \
    '*delay: 10000' '*ncolors: 64' '*cycles: 1' '*size: 100' \
    '*rotatepipes: False'
/tmp/pipes/prog 3000 1
```

Without `--incremental` it is Pipes as written. `HEAP=1` adds the host heap in
use after each frame; `ASAN=1` keeps AddressSanitizer on.

## What it changes, and why

- `pipes_incremental.h` is the experiment: an exact incremental redraw. Pipes
  clears and replays every piece's display list each frame, in order, under
  one camera, and adds one piece a frame. When the clear, both matrices and
  the lists so far match last frame, the canvas and z-buffer already hold
  them, so the wrapper skips the clear and those lists and replays only the
  new one. Anything else falls back to a real clear and a full replay.
- `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES`, which picks its triangle table
  (`teapot2.h`) over GL evaluators (`glMap2f`, `glEvalMesh2`), which TinyGL
  lacks.
- `buildlwo.c` is built with `GL_POLYGON` mapped to `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN`. TinyGL
  is built without `GL_POLYGON`, and an unhandled primitive keeps counting
  vertices past `c->vertex[3]` and overwrites the context: the lab crashed on
  frame 16 in `first_light`.

## Results (host, seed 1)

Frames are identical with and without the wrapper: every frame hash matched
over 600 frames, with the camera turning (the default, where the wrapper never
skips) and with it fixed.

| Settings | Extra host heap | Steady vertices a frame | Fade vertices a frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| As written (`cycles` 5, `size` 500), full redraw | about 44 MB | up to 977,000 | 977,000 |
| As written, incremental, camera fixed | about 44 MB | 380 | 977,000 |
| `cycles` 1, `size` 100, incremental, fixed | 1.2 to 1.7 MB | 307 | 32,200 |
| `cycles` 1, `size` 200, incremental, fixed | 2.7 to 3.6 MB | 327 | 69,800 |
| `cycles` 2, `size` 150, incremental, fixed | 4.4 to 4.9 MB | 321 | 100,400 |

- Extra heap is over a `size` 10 run (3.2 MB), and is mostly display lists.
  A list word (`GLParam`) holds a pointer, so it is 8 bytes on the host and 4
  on the board: halve these for the board. Pipes as written needs about 22 MB
  there, and the board has about 7 MB of PSRAM free. Pipes builds every list
  of a screen when the screen starts.
- A screen ends with a 25-frame fade that scales the whole picture, so every
  fade frame is a full redraw. At the #43 costs (4 us a vertex, 2.8 us more
  for each light on each lit vertex) a 32,200-vertex fade frame is about
  0.2 s.
- With the default turning camera every frame is a full redraw, so the
  wrapper never helps.

None of this has run on the board.

## Open decisions

- `buildlwo.c`, `buildlwo.h`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` carry no licence
  text. The repo's precedent for such files (Pacman's sprites, XMatrix's
  glyphs) is to read them from `vendor/` at build time and never commit them.
- A fixed camera (`*rotatepipes: False`) changes the look.
- The fade: keep it (about 5 s per screen at `size` 100), or end a screen
  without it.
- `GL_POLYGON` and `GL_LINE_LOOP` in TinyGL generally (see the #44 comment).

      52 docs/pipes-lab/lab_main.c
     115 docs/pipes-lab/pipes_incremental.h
      70 docs/pipes-lab/README.md

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAG

27	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
28	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
29	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
30	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
31	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
32	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
33	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
34	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
35	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
36	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
37	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
38	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
39	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
40	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
41	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
42	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
43	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
44	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
45	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
46	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
47	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
48	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
49	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
50	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
51	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
52	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
53	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
54	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
55	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
56	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
57	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
58	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
59	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
60	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
61	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
62	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
63	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
64	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
65	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
66	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
67	  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
68	  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
69	  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
70	  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
71	  new hack for both.
72	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
73	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
74	  neither.
75	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
76	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
77	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
78	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
79	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
80	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
81	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
82	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
83	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
84	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
85	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
86	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
87	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
88	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
89	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
90	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
91	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
92	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
93	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
94	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
95	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
96	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
97	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
98	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
99	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
100	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
101	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
102	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
103	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
104	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
105	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
106	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
107	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
108	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
109	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
110	  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
111	- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
112	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
113	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
114	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
115	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
116	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
117	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
118	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
119	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
120	  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
121	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
122	  to reach them.
123	- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
124	  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
125	  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
126	  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
127	  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
128	  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
129	  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
130	  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
131	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
132	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
133	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
134	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
135	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
136	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
137	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
138	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
139	  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
140	- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
141	  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
142	  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
143	  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
144	  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
145	  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
146	- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
147	  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
148	  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
149	  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
150	  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
151	  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
152	- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
153	  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
154	  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
155	  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
156	  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
157	- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
158	  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
159	  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
160	  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
161	  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
162	  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
163	  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
164	  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
165	  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
166	  drift from the firmware's rule.
167	- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
168	  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
169	  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
170	  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
171	  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
172	  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
173	  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
174	  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
175	  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
176	  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
177	  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
178	  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
179	  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
180	- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
181	  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
182	- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
183	  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
184	  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
185	  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
186	- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
187	  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
188	  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
189	  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
190	  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
191	  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
192	  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
193	- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
194	  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
195	  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
196	  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
197	  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
198	  the clears that ran, for the tests.
199	- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
200	  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
201	  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
202	  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
203	- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
204	  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
205	  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
206	  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
207	  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
208	  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
209	  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
210	- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
211	  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
212	  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
213	- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
214	  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
215	  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
216	  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
217	  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
218	  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
219	  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
220	  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
221	- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
222	  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
223	  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
224	  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
225	  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
226	  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
227	  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
228	  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
229	  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
230	- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
231	  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
232	  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
233	  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
234	  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
235	  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
236	  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
237	  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
238	- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
239	  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
240	  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
241	- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
242	  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
243	  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
244	  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
245	  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
246	  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
247	- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
248	  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
249	  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
250	  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
251	  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
252	- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
253	  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
254	  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
255	  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
256	  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
257	  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
258	  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
259	- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
260	  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
261	  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
262	- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
263	  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
264	  wrapper.

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
  wrapper.

/* Builds the unmodified blaster.c with a free that is safe before the first
 * draw. The hack sets NUM_ROBOTS in init but allocates `robots` on its first
 * draw, and its free loops NUM_ROBOTS times over `robots`, so freeing it first
 * dereferences NULL. Two quick button presses can do that. */
#include "screenhack.h"

/* blaster.c registers itself at its end; this file registers it instead. */
#undef XSCREENSAVER_MODULE
#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE(CLASS, PREFIX)

#include "blaster/blaster.c"

static void blaster_free_safe(Display *dpy, Window window, void *closure) {
  struct state *st = (struct state *)closure;
  if (!st->robots) st->NUM_ROBOTS = 0;
  blaster_free(dpy, window, closure);
}

const HackEntry blaster_hack = {"Blaster", blaster_defaults, blaster_init,
                                blaster_draw, blaster_free_safe};

static void blaster_free_safe(Display *dpy, Window window, void *closure) {

  if (!st->robots) st->NUM_ROBOTS = 0;

}
